intro: Joan Benson plays Bach’s late Fantasia in F♯ minor, Wq 67, on the clavichord, an instrument with a soft tone that can move suddenly from very soft to loud. Long runs extend beyond the bar lines, and short chords cut them off.

sections.label: A · Chords and free passagework
sections.mNote: Two measured bars of chords, then free passagework.

sections.label: B · Runs and quick exchanges
sections.mNote: Short figures join into longer passages of rapid notes.

sections.label: C · Short phrases separated by rests
sections.mNote: The clavichord plays short phrases with rests between them.

sections.label: D · Runs and accented chords
sections.mNote: Quick figures alternate with sharply accented chords.

sections.label: E · Quiet phrases and pauses
sections.mNote: Small gestures separated by pauses, in which the strings fade.

sections.label: F · Return of the running notes
sections.mNote: Flourishes alternate with chords on the keyboard

sections.label: Coda · Towards the final Largo
sections.mNote: The closing melody sounds over repeated F♯s.

cues.title: Opening bars, Adagio
cues.text: Adagio. Pairs of chords sound above a steady bass, separated by rests. After two measured bars a run rises through the keyboard and the bar lines stop. Sudden piano and forte markings alternate within a single phrase.
cues.evidence: Score, Liam Hynes transcription, p. 1, bars 1–3. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5b/IMSLP283144-PMLP459537-C.P.E._Bach_F-sharp_minor_Phantasy.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Benson’s first clavichord lessons
cues.text: Benson came to Fritz Neumeyer’s clavichord lessons as an accomplished pianist. At first he would not let her play pieces, and for months she worked only on producing a tone. Recalling those lessons in 1999, she said, “I had to become a beginner again”.
cues.evidence: Joan Benson interviewed by Richard Troeger, Boston Clavichord Society Newsletter 7, autumn 1999; recollection of lessons in Freiburg before 1960. https://joanbenson.com/articles-about-joan-benson/an-interview-with-clavichordist-joan-benson/

cues.title: Keyboard treatise, 1753
cues.text: “A musician cannot move others unless he too is moved.” Bach wrote this in his 1753 keyboard treatise. He named improvisations and fantasias as the places where the player could most directly command an audience’s feelings.
cues.evidence: C. P. E. Bach, Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, part I (1753), chapter 3, §13; William J. Mitchell translation (1948), p. 152, quoted in The Essential C. P. E. Bach, introduction, p. xix. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Charles Burney’s visit, Hamburg, 1772
cues.text: After dinner in Hamburg in 1772, Bach played the clavichord for Charles Burney until nearly eleven. Burney described his fixed eyes, his fallen lower lip and the sweat that gathered as he played.
cues.evidence: Charles Burney’s account of his 1772 visit, published in The Present State of Music in Germany, the Netherlands, and United Provinces (1775), vol. 2, p. 269; quoted in The Essential C. P. E. Bach, p. xiv. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Preparation for KQED broadcast, 1961
cues.text: Preparing this fantasia for a 1961 radio appearance on KQED, Benson considered shortening it but found that each section led into the next. In her 1999 interview with Richard Troeger, she recalled tracing the connection through the bass line and letting the piece change with every performance.
cues.evidence: Benson’s recollection of preparing Wq 67 for KQED in 1961, in Richard Troeger’s 1999 interview. https://joanbenson.com/articles-about-joan-benson/an-interview-with-clavichordist-joan-benson/

cues.title: First recording sessions, 1962
cues.text: Benson’s first recording sessions, in 1962, took place in three locations. Cleaners interrupted one and a radio station intruded on another, and the sessions were finally completed in a house in Marin County. Between takes she went outside to look at the stars or pet the dog.
cues.evidence: Benson recounts the 1962 Repertoire Records sessions to Richard Troeger in 1999. This is the history of her first record; the Commons transfer does not document its own session date. https://joanbenson.com/articles-about-joan-benson/an-interview-with-clavichordist-joan-benson/

cues.title: Final Largo over repeated F♯s
cues.text: The last Largo brings back bar lines and a twelve-eight metre. The left hand repeats low F♯s while the right hand plays its final figures. The last phrase is marked pianissimo, and rests follow the closing chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Accompanist to Frederick the Great and composer of keyboard music known for abrupt interruptions and trembling single notes.
facts: His father, Johann Sebastian Bach; studied law in Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder
Frederick II’s harpsichordist, 1740–67 · Hamburg music director, 1768–88
Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, 1753 and 1762
Wq: Alfred Wotquenne · H: E. Eugene Helm

quote.text: A musician can move others only if he is moved himself.
quote.source: Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Part I, chapter 3, §13 (1753); our translation

composer.background:
On 12 October 1772, Charles Burney dined with Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach in Hamburg. Bach’s wife, his lawyer son, his daughter and three or four friends were present; upstairs was a music room hung with pictures, drawings and prints of more than a hundred and fifty musicians. Before dinner Bach had played his Silbermann clavichord; after dinner Burney persuaded him to return to the keyboard, and he played until nearly eleven. As he played, his eyes became fixed and his lower lip dropped. Burney wrote that on a long note Bach could draw from the clavichord “a cry of sorrow and complaint”.

Emanuel was born in Weimar on 8 March 1714, the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara. Telemann was his godfather. The household moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, when Sebastian became Thomaskantor. Visiting musicians came to play for his father; the boy heard them at home. “In composition and keyboard playing I never had any teacher other than my father,” he wrote in the autobiography published in 1773.
